To form diminutives with -ino, -etto, -ello, -uccio: casetta, gattino, alberello.
To form augmentatives with -one (usually masculine): ragazzone, librone, portone.
To form pejoratives with -accio, -astro: tempaccio, parolaccia, giovinastro.
To recognise false alterations: mattone, bottone, tacchino, limone, burrone.
To use affectionate and polite diminutives: un attimino, un caffettino.
To know when NOT to use the suffixes (in the formal register, with certain words).

Sorrento, August. The trattoria is closed for the holidays, and the whole family has come to the seaside near Naples, where Giulia's grandmother, Assunta, is almost ninety-four. Assunta speaks only in diminutives.
Come here, big lad! Goodness, how you've grown. Last year you were a little boy.
Good morning, Signora Assunta. Does "ragazzone" mean I'm big?
Yes. "-one" makes things bigger. "Ragazzino" is a small boy, "ragazzone" a big boy.
And where's my little doll? Viola! Come to your great-granny, I'll give you a little biscuit.
Great-granny, little doll, little biscuit… Signora, you say everything small!
That's how we do it in Naples, young man. The things you love you make small, so they fit in your heart.
So is "mattone" a big madman? And "bottone" a big barrel?
No! Those are false alterations. "Mattone" means brick, and "bottone" means button. Like "tacchino", which isn't a little heel but a turkey.
And tonight, if the weather isn't nasty, I'll take you to eat a little pizza on the seafront.
Well done. Ugly weather, "tempaccio". Ugly word, "parolaccia". And you don't say swear words, do you?
Never, signora. Only a little bit, when Fiorentina lose.

The augmentative in -one often becomes MASCULINE, even if the base is feminine: la porta → il portone, la finestra → il finestrone, la palla → il pallone (the football).
"Ragazzaccio" can also be affectionate, said with a smile: "Vieni qua, ragazzaccio!" = Come here, you rascal!

For the first time in twenty years, Graziella closed the trattoria for two whole weeks in August. She hung a handwritten sign on the door, "Closed for holidays — ribollita back on the 25th", right under the new brass plaque, and got into the car with the face of someone going to the dentist. "Two weeks without cooking," she said to Marco, who was driving. "I don't know if I'll survive." Marco promised her that in Sorrento she could cook as much as she liked. He didn't yet know that this promise would start a war.

They had rented a little white house above the sea, with a small terrace full of geraniums and a little stone staircase leading down to the rocks. It was small, but they all fitted in: Graziella, Marco and Pietro upstairs, Matei, Giulia and Viola downstairs, Lupino everywhere. Ten minutes' walk away lived Giulia's cousin, and half an hour away by bus was Naples, where Grandma Assunta, almost ninety-four, had been waiting for months to finally meet "the famous ribollita cook".

Assunta arrived on the second day, accompanied by Gennaro and by Rosaria, Giulia's mother. She got out of the car leaning on a little dark wooden stick, looked at the house, looked at the sea, and then looked Graziella up and down, the way you look at a melon at the market. "So you're the lady with the little Tuscan soup," she said. Graziella, who had never heard her ribollita called "a little soup", smiled with all her teeth. "And you're the lady with the ragù," she replied. "I hear it's rather nice."

Giulia and Matei looked at each other. Gennaro let out a long whistle. Pietro, who had studied altered words with Giulia that very morning, immediately understood how serious the situation was. "Little soup" and "rather nice" were not affectionate diminutives. They were diminutives of war. "I reckon it's started," he whispered to Matei. Matei nodded. "Two grandmothers, one kitchen, fourteen days," he said. "Forget Caravaggio. This is an impossible restoration."

For the first few days the war stayed cold, fought only with words. Assunta called everyone by a diminutive: Viola was "my little doll", Pietro "the big lad", Matei "Mateuccio", Lupino "the little dog", even though Lupino now weighed twenty kilos. But Graziella was "the Florentine lady", with no diminutive at all. Graziella, for her part, called Assunta "the Neapolitan lady" and loudly praised the little pizzas on the seafront, "sweet, for such tiny little things".

Then, on the fifth day, the nasty weather arrived. A summer storm, the kind that reaches Sorrento from the sea in ten minutes, with a black sky and waves leaping over the rocks. No beach, no boat trip, no walk along the seafront. The whole family shut up in the little house, with the rain beating on the windows and Lupino hiding under a cot. It was then that Gennaro, bored, had the idea that changed the holiday. "Let's have a contest," he said. "Tonight each grandmother cooks her own dish. And Pietro judges."

"Me?" said Pietro, turning pale. "Why me?" "Because you're the only one who knows them both," explained Gennaro with Neapolitan logic. "And because you're a brave big lad." Pietro looked at Grandma Graziella, who was already tying on her apron, and at Grandma Assunta, who had already sent Rosaria to buy the meat. He realised there was no escape. "All right," he said. "But I want a contract. Like the one for Lupino. Whatever I decide, nobody gets angry."

The contract was written by Giulia on a little paper napkin and signed by everyone, Lupino included, with a sandy paw. Then the tiny kitchen of the little house became a battlefield. On one side Graziella, with the cavolo nero she had brought from Florence "just in case", the beans, the stale bread and the big pot. On the other Assunta, sitting on a chair because she couldn't stand for long, giving Rosaria orders for the ragù: "More onion. Less heat. Patience, my girl. Ragù isn't made, it's waited for."

For six hours the two grandmothers cooked side by side, barely speaking. But at a certain point, around five in the afternoon, something happened that nobody had foreseen. Graziella, tasting her broth, pulled a face. "Something's missing," she murmured. "In Florence I have my own oil. Here I don't know…" Assunta, without a word, got up with her stick, opened her bag and took out a little bottle. "Sorrento oil," she said. "From my cousin. Try it." Graziella hesitated. Then she poured a thread of it into the pot, tasted and closed her eyes.

"Delicious," she said. Not "rather nice". Delicious. Assunta pretended not to care, but Pietro saw that she was smiling. Half an hour later it was Graziella who returned the favour: Assunta's ragù needed basil, and in the little garden of the house, among the geraniums, Graziella had noticed a small plant. She picked three leaves and handed them to Assunta without a word. Assunta sniffed them, nodded and put them in the sauce. From that moment the two grandmothers began to talk to each other. First about oil and basil, then about pots, then about husbands.

When the family sat down to eat at half past eight, the rain had stopped and from the terrace you could see the clean gulf, with the lights of Naples in the distance. On the table were two big steaming pots and an empty little plate in front of Pietro, who had a napkin round his neck and the face of a judge in court. He tasted the ribollita. Then he drank a glass of water. Then he tasted the ragù, with the pasta Rosaria had cooked "al dente, as God commands". Then he drank another glass of water. Everyone was watching him. Lupino included.

Pietro stood up, took off his napkin and spoke as he had learned at the April meeting: in order, calmly, with the right words. "First of all, I thank the two cooks. Secondly, I must say something: Grandma Graziella's ribollita is the best in Florence. But tonight it has Sorrento oil in it. So it's the best ribollita in Florence and in Sorrento." Assunta raised an eyebrow. "And Grandma Assunta's ragù is the best in Naples," Pietro went on. "But tonight it has basil picked by Grandma Graziella. So it's a slightly Florentine ragù."

"In conclusion," he said, and made a dramatic pause he had seen Bellini make, "the contest is a draw. Because each of them won with a little piece of the other." There was a silence. Then Gennaro burst out laughing and started clapping, and after him everyone else. Assunta looked at Pietro with narrowed eyes. "Young man," she said, "you'll be a politician." "No, signora," replied Pietro. "I'll be a journalist. Politicians make promises. Journalists check whether they keep them."

That evening on the terrace, while the young ones washed the dishes, the two grandmothers sat side by side looking at the sea. Pietro, carrying out the glasses, heard them talking softly. Assunta was talking about her husband, who had been a fisherman and every evening brought her a little fish, "always the smallest, because he sold the big ones". Graziella was talking about Aldo and the ribollita he ate for a year. Then Assunta said something Pietro never forgot: "My dear lady, shy men are the best. Mine never once told me he loved me. He brought me a little fish every evening for sixty years."

The next day Assunta called Graziella by a diminutive for the first time. They were on the beach, under the umbrella, and Assunta offered her a little slice of watermelon. "Here you are, Graziellina," she said. Graziella took it, ate it and answered just as naturally: "Thank you, Assuntina." Rosaria, who was reading a newspaper next to them, looked up sharply, looked at Giulia and mouthed, without a sound: "Miracle." Giulia laughed. "No, Mum," she whispered. "Grammar. When a Neapolitan gives you a diminutive, it means you're family."

A few days later Gennaro took them all out in a boat, a little blue wooden boat belonging to a fisherman friend of his, to a small cave where the water was so clear you could see the little fish on the bottom. Viola, in her orange armbands, shouted "Fish-ino! Fish-ino!" at every fish that went by. Graziella, who had never been in a boat in her life, held on to the side with both hands and said she preferred the Arno, "which at least stays still". On the way back the fisherman gave Assunta a little silver fish, the smallest in the crate. Assunta looked at it for a long time, then gave it to Graziella without saying anything. Graziella understood. She cooked it that very evening, grilled, with a thread of Sorrento oil and a sprig of Tuscan rosemary, and divided it into two equal parts: one for herself, one for Assunta.

The rest of the holiday was one long lesson in altered words, in every direction. Viola learned to say "casetta", "gattino" and "pizzetta", and called everything she liked with an "-ino" on the end, even when it didn't exist: "sea-ino", "granny-ina", "Lupin-ino". In his notebook Pietro compiled a list of false alterations to show Davide, with drawings: a giant madman next to a brick, an enormous barrel next to a button, a tiny heel next to an angry turkey. Matei said they looked like surrealist paintings.

On the last evening there was another dinner, this time without a contest. Assunta and Graziella cooked together a dish that didn't exist in any recipe book: a ribollita with Sorrento tomatoes and a thread of the cousin's oil, served with Neapolitan bread. Gennaro christened it "la ribollitona", because it was enormous. Pietro protested that it was a false alteration, because it wasn't a big ribollita, it was a different ribollita. Gennaro replied that in Naples the rules of grammar are respected, yes, but with a pinch of imagination.

When they set off back to Florence on 24 August, Assunta saw them off in front of the little house, leaning on her stick. She hugged Viola, then Pietro, then Matei and Giulia. Last of all she hugged Graziella, for a long time. "Next year I'm coming to Florence," she said. "I want to see this famous trattoria with the plaque." "Next year you'll be ninety-five," Rosaria reminded her, worried. Assunta waved her hand as if shooing away a fly. "Exactly," she replied. "At ninety-five you don't wait. You go."

On 25 August, as the sign had promised, the trattoria in Via Maggio reopened. The first customer was Signor Franco, who came in at twelve on the dot and ordered ribollita. Graziella brought it and stood by the table, waiting. Franco tasted, stopped, tasted again. "Graziella," he said, puzzled, "there's something different. What have you put in it?" Graziella smiled and shrugged. "A little piece of Naples," she replied. "But don't tell anyone. It's a family secret."
